sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Amersfoort is in the middle of a contested switch to paid and permit parking. The car-light historic centre took effect on 4 January 2021, with access by exemption, permit-only street parking and 71 paid street spaces removed [0]. In November 2023 residents rejected the planned paid-parking policy in an advisory referendum, with about three quarters voting against, but the council amended and approved it on 22 April 2025: a first resident permit at 30 euros a year, a second at 300 euros in the centre or 150 at the edge, and visitors paying at most 1.20 euros a day [4][5]. Phase 1 started on 1 October 2025 in Kruiskamp, Gildekwartier and several other districts [6].

Phase 2 has slipped. On 11 December 2025 the alderman wrote that it would move from 1 February 2026 to 1 October 2026 for several districts [7]; after the March 2026 elections the city, on 8 April 2026, postponed paid parking in Soesterkwartier, Isselt, Eemkwartier, De Koppel and Liendert for the time being, keeping 1 October 2026 only for Jericho and Jeruzalem [7]. The northern districts will in any case not move to paid parking until 2035 according to RTV Utrecht [6]. Ahead of the March elections NOS reported that two local parties had been founded in protest [8]. The July 2026 coalition agreement states intentions to abolish the day ticket, charge 12 euros an hour for longer street stays near the centre, make the first two hours free in shopping areas that already have regulated parking and lower some tariffs; these are plans, not rules in force [9]. As of the page read in October 2026, street tariffs are 3 euros an hour in the hourly zones and a day ticket of 3 euros for the first hour then 60 euros [11], and permit tariffs are unchanged [13].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The coalition wants visitors to use garages in the centre, states that a garage should always be cheaper than the street and plans digital signs on the ring roads and a smart system showing garage availability; no system was found in operation [10]. The municipality stopped its earlier dynamic route information system in 2016, saying research had shown that displaying free spaces had almost no effect on garage choice [2]. The city says one public charge-point operator is currently active and places new points based on usage data [16]. Amersfoort has three P+R sites near stations, where rail travellers get a daily discount and P+R Schothorst now falls within paid parking on weekday nights [17].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The four municipality-linked garages, Koestraat (406 spaces), Flintplein (347), Amerena (218) and Stadhuisplein (177), are run by Coöperatie ParkeerService, are open 24/7 and use plate recognition at exit [14]; Koestraat and Stadhuisplein charge 3.24 euros an hour and Flintplein 2.61, all with a daily maximum of 16.22 euros [12]. Other garages include Eemplein (625 spaces, managed by Parkking), Q-Park Mondriaan (575), St. Jorisplein (462) and Beestenmarkt (365), and P1's Asch van Wijckstraat (450) [15]. A December 2021 audit by the city's audit office counted 13 public garages with 4,571 spaces in use on 1 December 2019 and found that the municipality had only limited occupancy information even for its own garages [1][3]; these figures are old.

Our data cover two park-and-ride sites, Barchman Wuijtierslaan (260 spaces) and Piet Mondriaanplein (491), measured for 61 days since 22 August 2026. Occupancy averaged only about 16% on weekdays and 12% at weekends, weighted by spaces. Barchman Wuijtierslaan averaged 25% on weekdays and reached 82% on a Thursday morning, while Piet Mondriaanplein averaged 11% and never exceeded 41%. We have no readings for the centre garages. The window includes the end of the summer holidays.
